lead: A real wing box has a skin stiffened by many stringers, and integrating the shear flow round it by hand is long. Structural idealisation replaces it by booms, concentrated areas that carry all the direct stress, joined by thin panels that carry only shear. Each boom stands for a stringer plus the skin working with it. Done properly, the idealised section has the same second moment as the real one, and the shear flow becomes a short sum.
prereq: You need: the bending stress in thin-walled sections, and the shear flow jump at a boom from the chapter on open sections.

sections.h3: Booms carry direct stress, panels carry shear

blocks.text: In a stiffened skin most of the direct stress is carried by the stringers, spar caps and the strip of skin next to them. The skin between stringers is thin and carries little direct stress, but it carries shear well. The idealised section keeps that split: each stringer and its share of skin becomes a boom of area B at the stringer position, and each length of skin between booms becomes a panel of the real thickness t that carries a constant shear flow.

Panels that keep part of their skin in the booms are called effective in bending, through the boom areas. A wall given no boom contribution at all, such as a thin web between booms that already include the spar caps, is ineffective in bending: it carries shear only and adds nothing to I. Both kinds still enter ∮ds/t in twist calculations.

Take a skin panel of width b and thickness t between booms 1 and 2, with direct stresses σ₁ and σ₂ at its edges and a linear variation between them. Replace it by two areas at its edges that give the same force and the same moment about each edge. That gives, for boom 1:

blocks.where: B₁ is the boom area at edge 1 contributed by this panel (mm²); t is the panel thickness and b its width (mm); σ₂/σ₁ is the ratio of the direct stresses at the far and near edges.

blocks.text: A boom collects one such term from every panel it touches, plus its own stringer or spar-cap area. Two ratios occur often. A skin panel between two booms at the same height under bending has σ₂/σ₁ = 1, so it contributes t b/2 to each. A spar web from the top boom to the bottom boom has σ₂/σ₁ = −1, so it contributes only t b/6 to each. For a stringer on a straight run between two equal panels of pitch p, the two terms add to t p.

items: Mark every stringer and spar cap as a boom.
For each boom, list the panels it touches, their widths and thicknesses.
Find σ₂/σ₁ for each panel from the bending case (the ratio of the boom distances from the neutral axis for pure M<sub>x</sub>).
B = stringer area + Σ (t b/6)(2 + σ₂/σ₁) over the panels.
Check: Σ B y² should equal the exact I<sub>xx</sub> of the real section.

sections.h3: Properties, stresses and shear flows of the idealised section

blocks.text: I<sub>xx</sub> = Σ B<sub>r</sub> y<sub>r</sub>²,   σ<sub>r</sub> = M<sub>x</sub> y<sub>r</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub>
blocks.where: I<sub>xx</sub> is the idealised second moment (mm⁴); B<sub>r</sub> and y<sub>r</sub> are the area (mm²) and distance from the neutral axis (mm) of boom r; σ<sub>r</sub> is the boom stress (N/mm²); M<sub>x</sub> is the bending moment (N·mm).
the jump in panel shear flow across boom r (N/mm) for a section symmetric about x; S<sub>y</sub> is the shear force (N). Between booms q is constant.

blocks.text: A closed idealised box is solved exactly as in the closed-section chapter: cut a panel, sum the jumps, add q<sub>s,0</sub>. If the box is symmetric about the vertical axis and the load acts on that axis, the cut can be put on the axis of symmetry where q is zero, and no q<sub>s,0</sub> is needed. The panel stress is τ = q/t.

figure.caption: The worked example idealised. Each corner boom takes its spar cap plus a third of the 200 mm skin panel (ratio +1) and a sixth of the web (ratio −1); the mid-stringer takes a third of each skin panel either side. The six booms give exactly the real I<sub>xx</sub>, and a 15 kN shear puts 12.25 N/mm in each skin panel and 37.5 N/mm in each web.

examples.question: A wing box has a rectangular mid-line 400 mm wide and 200 mm deep. Its four spar caps are 300 mm² each, and one stringer of 150 mm² sits at mid-width of the top skin and another at mid-width of the bottom skin. The skins and the spar webs are all 2 mm thick. Idealise it into six booms, check I<sub>xx</sub> against the real section, and find the boom stresses for M<sub>x</sub> = 30 kN·m and the panel shear flows for S<sub>y</sub> = 15 kN through the vertical axis of symmetry.
steps: Skin panels are 200 mm wide (corner to mid-stringer) with σ₂/σ₁ = 1; each spar web is 200 mm deep with σ₂/σ₁ = −1.
Real section: skins 2 × 400 × 2 × 100² = 1.6 × 10⁷; webs 2 × 2 × 200³/12 = 2,666,667; caps and stringers (4 × 300 + 2 × 150) × 100² = 1.5 × 10⁷. Total 3.3667 × 10⁷ mm⁴: the same.

Boom stresses: σ = M<sub>x</sub> y/I<sub>xx</sub> = 30 × 10⁶ × 100/3.3667 × 10⁷ = ±89.1 N/mm²: with M<sub>x</sub> positive (top in tension in this convention) +89.1 in the top booms and −89.1 in the bottom booms.

Shear: S<sub>y</sub>/I<sub>xx</sub> = 4.4554 × 10⁻⁴ N/mm³. By symmetry the top skin flow is equal and opposite either side of the mid-stringer, so the mid-boom jump 24.50 N/mm splits into 12.25 N/mm in each top panel.
Each spar web: 12.25 + 4.4554 × 10⁻⁴ × 566.7 × 100 = 37.50 N/mm, and the bottom panels carry 12.25 N/mm. Check: 2 webs × 37.50 × 200 = 15,000 N = S<sub>y</sub>.
examples.answer: Corner booms 566.7 mm², mid booms 550.0 mm², I<sub>xx</sub> = 3.3667 × 10⁷ mm⁴ (exact); boom stresses ±89.1 N/mm²; 12.25 N/mm in each skin panel and 37.50 N/mm in each web.

traps: Using σ₂/σ₁ = +1 for a spar web. The web runs from tension to compression, so the ratio is −1; +1 gives a corner boom of 700 mm² instead of 566.7 and an I<sub>xx</sub> that is too large.
Giving a straight-run stringer only half the skin. It collects a term from the panel on each side: t p in total for equal panels.
Deleting the panel once its skin is in the boom. The panel still carries the shear flow.
Adding panel areas into Σ B y in the shear sum. Only booms change q.

quiz.q: What does a boom carry, and what does a panel carry, in an idealised section?
quiz.a: A boom carries direct (axial) stress only; a panel carries shear flow only, constant along its length.

quiz.q: Why does a spar web contribute less to each boom than a skin panel of the same size?
quiz.a: Its direct stress varies from tension at one boom to compression at the other, so σ₂/σ₁ = −1 and each boom gets t b/6. A skin panel at one height has σ₂/σ₁ = 1 and gives t b/2.

quiz.q: A stringer of 120 mm² has 1.5 mm skin panels 80 mm wide on each side, at the same stress. Find B.
Four booms of 500 mm² sit at y = ±150 mm. Find I<sub>xx</sub> and the web flow for S<sub>y</sub> = 20 kN in a two-web box.
In the example, why are the top skin flows not zero, as they would be in a four-boom box?
quiz.a: The mid-stringer boom has area, so q jumps by 24.50 N/mm across it. By symmetry the two halves carry ±12.25 N/mm. With no boom at mid-width the jump is zero and so are the skin flows.

quiz.q: For pure torque, does the idealisation change the shear flow?
quiz.a: No. A single cell under torque has q = T/2A whatever the booms; only the enclosed area and ∮ds/t matter.

beyond: Not for the exam. Finite element models of wing boxes use rod elements for stringers and shear panels for skins, the same split. Search for "shear panel and rod idealisation".
